human_review: [test/inductor/test_aot_inductor.py] if you have `binary_blob` constant format, then the compiled .so should have `USE_MMAP_EXTERNAL` flag, and the model should use `user_managed_mmap` but not `self_mmap`? Then the changed code chunk should never be reached.

[test/inductor/test_aot_inductor.py] even if you do not use the binary_blob format, and used None, which means you do not package weight on disk, then the code chunk you modified will be reached. 

But then, the code that write the weight blob is here:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f5291ea9c4bb6ea2c3e941e3eb8430045fd21b25/torch/_inductor/codecache.py#L2588-L2596

When the page size is greater than 16k, it should still be aligned with the page size. 

looks like it's enough to just change the AOTI_RUNTIME_CHECK to check if weights_offset is aligned with either 16k or page size

[test/inductor/test_aot_inductor.py] thanks for the catch @yushangdi 

the test wasn't actually exercising the fix. on 64k systems, the py codecache already aligns weights to 64k at compile time, so the offset would always be aligned - the fix's adjustment logic never kicks in.

i updated the test to simulate this by patching `resource.getpagesize()` to return 4096 during compilation. this forces 16K alignment, creating a misaligned offset (e.g., 0x58000) that would fail on 64k systems without the fix.

i also tested on GH200 (aarch64, 64K pages):
`without fix: mmap(..., 0x58000) = -1 EINVAL`
`with fix: loads successfully`

please do take a look and lmk!
[torch/csrc/inductor/aoti_runtime/model_base.h] Shouldn't this be gated behind `#ifdef __LINUX__`? and assume page size is 4K on other platforms?

human_review: [test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] Let's also add an or condition for `PLATFORM_SUPPORTS_SYMM_MEM ` that will ensure we don't run these on mi200. Symm Mem is not supported on MI200.

[torch/distributed/_symmetric_memory/_rocshmem_triton.py] A little confused here. If it is a true inheritance case, then we'd have all common code in _shmem_triton and _shmem_triton would include either _rocshmem_triton or _nvshmem_triton based on the backend. If _shmem_triton includes _rocshmem_triton and _rocshem_triton includes _shmem_triton, then we'd be in circular dependency loop.
[torch/distributed/_symmetric_memory/_shmem_triton.py] I feel all code here should just be if hip: call rocshmem variant else: call nvshmem variant
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] this can be directly imported as before.
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] we use `skipIfRocm` or `skipCUDAIfRocm`. However, for UT classes inheriting from MultiProcContinuousTest, we use `skip_if_rocm_multiprocess`
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] Why are we renaming this UT and also not feeling comfortable with removing all the other decorators.
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] Can we use the enum name instead ?
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] these barriers required? It seems like cheating if we are needing extra barriers to get right results. This means something is not right in code.
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] same comment as above, not comfortable removing requires_h100 from here.
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] Please use `skip_rocm_multiprocess`
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] This makes it hard to read and understand where the code is supposed to run. Lets add requires_h100 back to all the UTs.
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] sure, I can add back requires_h100

[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] the sporadic hang issue is confirmed resolved with fixing rocshmem_barrier_all_wg API and using correct NVSHMEM_SIGNAL_ADD value for rocSHMEM, so these barriers are no longer required
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] reverted to original implementation, it seems unnecessary now
[test/distributed/test_shmem_triton.py] we don't have python binding or wrapper to expose them via c++ header, so direct enum cant be referenced here, will document the source for reference

[torch/distributed/_symmetric_memory/_rocshmem_triton.py] Instead of seeing this as pure inheritance, it is more like shared utilities between 2 backends, 
 _shmem_triton.py - Earlier version mixed 2 things: 
1.  Shared utilities (one-way dependency) - being imported by `_rocshmem_triton`
  -- ShmemKernelRegistry
  -- run_shmem_init_hook()
  -- build_requires_shmem_decorator()

 2. Dispatch function - requires_shmem, get_shmem_backend_module - which was creating backward reference to backend module to get either nvshmem or rocshmem 

Earlier change created circular dependency due to that.

I tried to address it in a cleaner way as you suggested to keep backend specific redirection in _shmem_triton.py and that abstracts away backend selection for end user. Shared utilities were moved to _rocshmem_triton.py for now to self-contain. 

Later we can create another _shmem_triton_utils.py to hold common shared utilities between nvshmem and rocshmem. It would not depend on anything else, that can be used by _rocshmem_triton / _nvshmem_triton to avoid some duplication and that will also avoid circular dependency that we saw with previous version.

title: Add pluggable MaterializeFn hook to StorageImpl
human_review: [c10/core/StorageMaterializer.h] Why not use a proper movable std::function?
[c10/core/StorageImpl.h] Why not also have this be part of ctor I guess?

[c10/core/StorageMaterializer.h] Right, I kept it minimal and avoiding the heap allocation overhead in the hot-path. The materializer has access to all the embedded state in the DataPtr context, so I figured a simple 8-byte raw function pointer should suffice without the extra machinery on a hot path. Let me know if you still feel strongly about it. The nice thing is that if needing to switch to std::function later, it would remain backward-compatible for any accelerator extensions outside of PT.

[c10/core/StorageImpl.h] Great point. The existing hooks (`set_throw_on_mutable_data_ptr`, `set_warn_deprecated_on_mutable_data_ptr`) are all attached post-construction, and materializers follow the same pattern: `lazy_clone_storage()` creates the storage obj first, then wraps it. I could add a ctor parameter, but it would be more invasive for this PR and feel bloated given that COW attachment is fairly granular (and future use cases would be too). Longer term, we could refactor toward a single context-based ctor arg that captures these options together.
[c10/core/StorageImpl.h] Why forward declaration here? Cycle?

[c10/core/StorageMaterializer.h] I prefer raw function pointer as well. However, I'd prefer not to pass by mutable reference; it's more idiomatic to pass a non-const StorageImpl pointer per the current codebase.
[c10/core/StorageImpl.h] It would have been better to not do this rename, or do it separately, adds a lot of review fuzz

[c10/core/StorageImpl.h] I don't understand the error here. If it is always correct to call `clear_materializer` first, then this function should just do that (you're paying for the conditional anyway). If it's not always correct, the error message shouldn't suggest it unconditionally.
[c10/core/impl/COW.cpp] Assert it.

[c10/core/StorageImpl.h] Seems like one of the implied goals of this PR was to remove `StorageImpl.h`'s dependence on `COW.h` and `COWDeleter.h`. But in order for `materialize_cow` to work, it still needs to be a friend of `StorageImpl`, so it needs to be declared. So I guess we can't really fully remove dependence on `COW.h`, and I wonder if it would be simpler for this this file to just keep the `#include <c10/core/impl/COW.h>`, rather than have two identical declarations of `materialize_cow` in separate parts of the codebase

[torch/csrc/Module.cpp] There's a pybind function later on in this file, `_is_cow_tensor`, which is used for testing. It calls `c10::impl::cow::is_cow_data_ptr`. Now that `COW.h` is not included in `StorageImpl.h`, this include needed to be added

[c10/core/StorageImpl.h] I agree, but kept it in the same commit, as it's partially due to the rename being semantically tied to this change, as the method now dispatches through the generic `MaterializeFn` hook rather than calling COW logic directly.

[c10/core/StorageImpl.h] Yes, it's to avoid a cycle. COW.h/COW.cpp depend on StorageImpl, so including COW.h from StorageImpl.h would be circular. The forward decl exists only to support the friend declaration, which materialize_cow needs to access the protected method set_data_ptr_no_materialize.

I could also make `set_data_ptr_no_materialize` public instead, so wouldn't need the friend declaration nor that fwd declaration. No strong preference here.

[torch/csrc/Module.cpp] This file calls [cow::is_cow_data_ptr()](https://github.com/rpsilva-aws/pytorch/blob/194e5a72c337a2386360587eacbd8dbc267d8019/torch/csrc/Module.cpp#L2970). It was previously included transitively via StorageImpl.h in COW.h. Now that StorageImpl no longer includes COW.h, the explicit include was needed.

[c10/core/StorageImpl.h] Hmm, but `COW.h` already forward declares `StorageImpl` in order to avoid a cycle, so it isn't truly a cycle if `StorageImpl.h` includes `COW.h`, right? It just feels like it's not necessary to have forward declarations in both files, unless I'm missing something. I don't feel strongly about this though
This seems basically fine.
Nice improvement!

+import weakref
+from enum import auto, Enum

+    PYTHON = auto()

+    GRAD_FN_HOOK = auto()
+    GRAD_FN_HOOK_CAPTURES_GRAD_FN = auto()
+    POST_ACCUMULATE_GRAD = auto()

+    BACKWARD = auto()
+    RETAIN_GRAPH = auto()

+    @staticmethod

+
+    @staticmethod

+
+    @staticmethod

+        return grad * 2
+

+    """Custom function that saves its output."""

+    @staticmethod
+    def forward(ctx, x):
+        y = x.exp()
+        ctx.save_for_backward(y)
+        return y

+    @staticmethod

+        return grad * y

+class PythonSplit(Function):
+    """Custom function with two outputs."""

+    @staticmethod
+    def forward(ctx, x):

+    @staticmethod

+

+

+
+
+class TestNodeLifecycle(TestCase):
+    """Single output, various node types / hooks / backward states."""
+
+    def _run(self, node_type, hook_type, backward_state):
+        a = torch.randn(4, requires_grad=True)

+        marker_ref = weakref.ref(marker)
+
+        grad_fn = b.grad_fn
+
+        if hook_type == HookType.TENSOR_HOOK:

+
+            b.register_hook(hook)
+        elif hook_type == HookType.TENSOR_HOOK_CAPTURES_GRAD_FN:
+
+            def hook(grad):
+                grad_fn
+                marker
+
+            b.register_hook(hook)
+        elif hook_type == HookType.GRAD_FN_HOOK:
+
+            def hook(*args):
+                marker
+
+            b.grad_fn.register_hook(hook)
+        elif hook_type == HookType.GRAD_FN_HOOK_CAPTURES_GRAD_FN:
+
+            def hook(*args):

+                marker
+
+            b.grad_fn.register_hook(hook)
+

+            b.sum().backward()
+        elif backward_state == BackwardState.RETAIN_GRAPH:

+def _major_label(is_k_major, other_major):

+
+
+def _normalize_major(value):
+    return value.replace("-", "").replace("_", "")

+
+def _parse_tensor_spec(value, allowed_majors, expected_str, example):
+    value = value.lower()
+    try:
+        dim_str, layout_str = value.split(":")
+    except ValueError as exc:
+        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(
+            f"Expected {expected_str} (e.g., {example})."
+        ) from exc

+        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(f"Expected {expected_str} (e.g., {example}).")
+    major_norm = _normalize_major(layout_str)
+    if major_norm not in allowed_majors:
+        raise argparse.ArgumentTypeError(f"Expected {expected_str} (e.g., {example}).")
+    return (int(dim_str[0]), major_norm == "kmajor")
+
+

+    if align == 1:

[aten/src/ATen/native/mps/operations/LinearAlgebra.mm] **<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Parse GEMM preference env var as boolean value**

`PYTORCH_MPS_GEMM_PREFER_FAST_MATH` is read with `has_env`, so any defined value (including `0`) enables the GEMM override. In environments that export boolean flags as `0/1`, setting `PYTORCH_MPS_GEMM_PREFER_FAST_MATH=0` still disables `force_metal` when `PYTORCH_MPS_PREFER_METAL` and `PYTORCH_MPS_FAST_MATH` are set, causing GEMM to unexpectedly stop using Metal kernels. This makes the new flag impossible to turn off via a `0` value and can silently change backend/performance behavior.

title: Fix ConvTranspose3d complex half accuracy by promoting 3D transposed complex convolution to double
human_review: [aten/src/ATen/native/Convolution.cpp] We should avoid doing this in native convolution, which is the main entry and would impact all backends.

[aten/src/ATen/native/Convolution.cpp] @guangyey, thanks for the feedback. 
I changed the approach and moved the fix from the generic complex_convolution path into conv_transpose3d_symint, so it is now limited to ConvTranspose3d complex-half only. 

An XPU-only fix is not possible here because complex inputs are already decomposed in the shared composite path before backend dispatch, so XPU no longer sees the original complex-half type.

[aten/src/ATen/native/Convolution.cpp] I am not sure whether I miss something. If `ConvTranspose3d` has accuracy issue for half complex in XPU, we should know the root cause (oneDNN or PyTorch) rather than workaround it. We shouldn't add this logic for XPU, which would impact all backends until we know the root cause and have to do this.

[aten/src/ATen/native/Convolution.cpp] Root cause is numerical, not XPU-specific: complex32 transposed convolution relies on Gauss decomposition (three real convolutions + recombination), which in low precision amplifies rounding/cancellation error.
Promoting complex32 inputs to complex128 for compute, then casting back to complex32, stabilizes numerics and restores CPU-XPU parity.
After deeper analysis, the same mechanism applies to conv_transpose1d and conv_transpose2d as well, not only conv_transpose3d.
@guangyey , what do you think about applying the same fix to 1d/2d for consistency?

Given different functions `f1` and `f2`, your PR makes `wrap_inline(f1)` and `wrap_inline(f2)` have different code objects. Wouldn't that _trigger_ recompilation (as opposed to "don't recompile" as you documented)?

I think I got it, by returning a new code object, you are changing recompilations into compilation over _different_ frames (i.e., code objects).

So this is mainly for compiling a `wrap_inline`-ed function at top level (or after graph breaks, however that might get triggered). But you still want to treat different instances of `wrap_inline(f)`s (with same input function object) as the same frame for compilation (basically my example), thus the cache.

## Pull request overview

This PR adjusts the PyTorch test suite’s pytest configuration timing to avoid a signal-handler race between early GPU/runtime initialization triggered by `torch.testing._internal.common_utils` import side effects and pytest’s built-in `faulthandler` plugin initialization.

**Changes:**
- Defers the lazy import + invocation of `parse_cmd_line_args()` from `pytest_configure` to `pytest_sessionstart`.
- Wraps the import/call in a small helper (`_call_parse_cmd_line_args`) to keep the import deferred and contained.

From what I could find [here](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/issues/3261#issuecomment-369740536) is the order of the pytest hooks.

> Because the globals set by parse_cmd_line_args are only consumed during actual test execution, deferring this setup to pytest_sessionstart is safe and does not affect test behavior.

That's not entirely true: some tests are instantiated / parameterised based on some of the values in common_utils / cmd line args but as long as `parse_cmd_line_args()` is called before test collect  I think we're fine.
